\section{Cross-lingual transfer of variable roles}
\label{sec:crosslang}

XLCoST implements the same algorithm in several languages, and its
\texttt{problem\_id} is a hash of the problem description, so the same
identifier names a problem in every language that implements it. That makes
it possible to hold meaning constant and vary surface form---the manipulation
a typological question needs. We exploit it to ask what actually transfers
when a variable-role classifier is moved across languages.

\paragraph{Only three languages are genuinely parallel.} Shared problem ids
are abundant for Python/JavaScript/PHP ($2{,}953$, $1{,}529$ and $1{,}145$
pairwise) and scarce for every other pair in XLCoST. We computed the full
$6\times 6$ overlap matrix rather than one row of it
(\texttt{results/lp4fm/xlcost\_problem\_overlap.csv}), because the limitation
it documents is stronger than a note about Python: \emph{no} pair outside this
triangle reaches $500$ shared problems, including pairs that share a language
family. Java and JavaScript share $85$ problems, C++ and JavaScript $75$, and
even C\# and Java---both C-family, both statically typed---share only $175$ of
roughly $9{,}000$.
Unmatched transfer confounds ``roles do not transfer'' with ``different
problems,'' so we report the matched triangle and treat the rest as
unavailable rather than weak.

\paragraph{A model-free baseline that also transfers.} For each ordered pair
we fit a character $n$-gram classifier on the source language and evaluate it
on the target, over the same problems, with the variable's own name masked.
The vectoriser is fitted on the source alone: whatever character structure
carries the label in one language must be present in the other for this to
score above chance. Table~\ref{tab:crosslang} reports the strongest such
feature.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-lingual role transfer over all six ordered pairs of
Python/JavaScript/PHP, matched on shared problems. \emph{Masked} is a
character $n$-gram classifier with no model and the variable's own name
removed; \emph{probe} is a linear probe on the residual stream of
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, fitted on the source language and evaluated on the target.
Both are computed on the same capped sample. Note the ranges, not just the
maxima: the baseline spans $0.39$ macro-F1, the probe $0.11$.}
\label{tab:crosslang}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
role & masked-context & probe & majority & shuffled labels \\
\midrule
accumulator & 0.736--0.954 & 0.833--0.918 & 0.271--0.415 & 0.439--0.504 \\
index\_key  & 0.839--0.964 & 0.854--0.915 & 0.314--0.419 & 0.459--0.516 \\
iterator    & 0.576--\textbf{0.965} & 0.851--0.939 & 0.428--0.475 & 0.438--0.488 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Transfer reaches macro-F1 $0.965$ without a language model and without the
variable's name. The name alone is the strongest feature in only $6$ of $18$
cells, so this is not simply shared identifier conventions: it is the
surrounding code. Resolution is not the limiting factor---one test occurrence
of the smallest class moves macro-F1 by $\rho \in [0.0003, 0.0020]$ here,
because these folds hold thousands of occurrences, and the smallest effect in
the table---measured against its own shuffled-label control, as in
\texttt{results/lp4fm/SUMMARY.md}---clears the largest $\rho$ by a factor
of $57$.

\paragraph{Transfer is asymmetric, along a typological axis.} Two comparisons
make the point, and they are distinct. Holding the source fixed, iterator
transfers from PHP to JavaScript at $0.965$ but from PHP to Python at
$0.576$: the same trained classifier, applied to a brace language and to an
indentation language, differing by $0.39$. Holding the \emph{pair} fixed and
reversing direction, Python$\rightarrow$PHP reaches $0.741$ while
PHP$\rightarrow$Python reaches $0.576$, a gap of $0.165$---so the asymmetry
is directional, not merely a property of which languages are involved.

In both comparisons the pairs sharing C-family statement syntax transfer
better, and every poor cell involves Python. This is a property of the
languages, not of the surface model, and it is the clearest evidence in this
study that what $n$-grams transfer is surface structure.

One confound deserves stating, because the corpus invites it. XLCoST does not
deliver these languages in the same shape: Python comes from the formatted
mirror with real newlines and indentation, while JavaScript and PHP come from
the tokenized one and arrive flattened onto a single line ($100\%$ and $98\%$
of programs contain no newline at all). The typological boundary and the
corpus-provenance boundary are the same line, so a classifier keying on layout
would produce this pattern without any linguistic content. It cannot: the
character analyser collapses whitespace runs before forming $n$-grams, so line
structure never becomes a feature, and normalising whitespace on both sides
changes the transfer scores by less than $0.001$. We therefore describe the
contrast in terms of statement syntax rather than block delimiters, which is
what the features can actually see.

\paragraph{The probe is flat exactly where the baseline collapses.} Running a
linear probe on the residual stream over the identical cells does not
uniformly beat the surface baseline, and the pattern of where it wins is the
result. Split the eighteen cells by whether Python is involved:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & JavaScript$\leftrightarrow$PHP & pairs involving Python & change \\
\midrule
masked-context & 0.952 & 0.785 & $-0.166$ \\
probe          & 0.893 & 0.887 & $-0.006$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent The division is total: the baseline beats the probe in all six cells
of the typologically close pair, and the probe beats the baseline in all twelve
cells involving Python, with no exceptions. Every one of the eighteen gaps
clears its own $\rho$, the smallest ($0.015$) by a factor of $3.8$.

\paragraph{Why the surface baseline fails to cross, mechanically.} The
asymmetry above is an observation with a label attached to it. Because the
baseline fits its vectorizer on the source language and only calls
\texttt{transform} on the target, an $n$-gram the target never realises
contributes exactly zero to every target prediction, which makes the
mechanism measurable rather than merely nameable. Two candidate explanations
fail, and the one that survives is not the one the label suggests.

The obvious explanation---the discriminative $n$-grams are missing from the
target---is wrong. Weighting each feature by $|\beta_j|$ times its mean
tf-idf, roughly $70\%$ of the source classifier's discriminative mass is
realised in \emph{every} target, including those it transfers to worst
($0.696$ for php$\rightarrow$python against $0.735$ for
php$\rightarrow$javascript). Across the six ordered pairs, surviving mass
does not predict transfer at all ($r = +0.09$).

What predicts it is whether the surviving features mean the same thing.
Fitting a second classifier on the target labels in the \emph{same} feature
space and correlating the two weight vectors, weighted by the source's
reliance on each feature, gives an agreement that tracks transfer closely
($r = +0.89$; the mass of features whose sign flips tracks it inversely,
$r = -0.82$). Between JavaScript and PHP agreement is $0.93$ and $0.91$ with
only about $6.5\%$ of the mass flipping sign; every pair crossing the Python
boundary sits between $0.37$ and $0.61$ with $28$--$40\%$ flipping. The cues
are present on both sides and they point different ways.

That realignment is distributed rather than localised, which is the result
that most constrains the interpretation. Masking a whole syntactic character
class on \emph{both} sides---terminators, braces, brackets, parentheses, or
operators---changes transfer by at most $0.021$ in any condition, against a
gap of $0.39$ to be explained. Masking braces costs php$\rightarrow$javascript
$0.001$. So the difference is not carried by block delimiters or statement
terminators, and describing it as a brace-versus-indentation contrast would
be wrong even though that contrast is real in the languages.

We deliberately stop short of naming individual $n$-grams. The largest
sign-flips are identifier and literal fragments rather than syntax, which
invites a story about naming idiom, but the story does not survive checking:
the variable \texttt{i} carries the iterator label at $0.67$, $0.61$ and
$0.64$ of its occurrences in PHP, JavaScript and Python respectively, so its
flipped weight is not a difference in what \texttt{i} does. Individual
coefficients of a regularised model over heavily correlated character
$n$-grams are not interpretable one at a time, and we report the aggregate,
which is.

\paragraph{Flatness is only a finding above an untrained floor.} Two
observations make that qualification necessary rather than decorative. First,
a model trained without code---Qwen2.5-1.5B, identical to the code model in
architecture, scale and tokenizer---is equally flat, averaging $0.892$ against
the code model's $0.889$. Code pretraining is therefore not what produces the
language-independent representation. Second, once two very differently trained
models give indistinguishable numbers, the natural worry is that neither is
doing the work: a linear probe over pooled token representations might recover
role from any encoder, in which case the flatness would be a fact about our
inputs and not about a model.

We ran the control that separates these. An untrained network of the same
architecture, same tokenizer and randomly initialised weights reaches $0.575$,
against $0.889$ and $0.892$ for the trained models---a gap of $0.314$, present
in all eighteen cells, with a minimum per-cell lift of $0.126$. The untrained
network is itself flat, dropping $0.021$ across the typological boundary, which
is the point: flatness alone is cheap, because a network that cannot separate
the roles in any language is trivially insensitive to which language it fails
in. What distinguishes the trained models is that they are flat \emph{and}
high. The untrained network is not at chance either---it clears its own
shuffled control by $0.111$, as random projections of token identity should---so
$0.575$, not $0.5$, is the floor a representational claim has to clear.

The two rows say different things. Between JavaScript and PHP---both C-family,
both brace-delimited---character $n$-grams already reach $0.952$, and the
residual stream adds nothing to a signal the surface has saturated. Across the
typological boundary the baseline loses $0.166$ while the probe loses $0.006$.
The extreme case is iterator from PHP to Python, where the baseline falls to
$0.576$ and the probe holds at $0.865$. Across all eighteen cells the
baseline's spread is $0.390$ and the probe's is $0.107$: the surface measure
varies $3.7\times$ as much as the representational one.

So the asymmetry of the previous paragraph is a property of the surface, not
of the representation. Under the probe, the same two comparisons that differed
by $0.389$ and $0.165$ differ by $-0.013$ and $+0.038$---the typological axis
essentially disappears. The model's contribution is not a uniform increment; it
is inversely proportional to how much surface similarity the language pair
already provides. Controls behave: source-shuffled probes score $0.434$--$0.512$,
and in-domain probes on the source language reach $0.877$--$0.985$, so the
cross-lingual numbers are not an artifact of a probe that fits anything.

\paragraph{Renaming separates lexical from structural transfer.} We rename
the source language before training---C1 replaces every local with
\texttt{v1, v2, \dots}, C2 with \texttt{a, b, c, \dots}, C4 with random
nouns---and leave the target untouched. The variable's own name is masked in
the features either way, so what changes is the \emph{surrounding}
identifiers. A signal that survives is carried by structure; one that
collapses was lexical. Table~\ref{tab:crosslang-rename} reports how much of
each role's headroom over its own shuffled control survives.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Headroom over the shuffled-label control retained after renaming the
source language (mean over C1, C2, C4 and both targets; the renamer supports
Python, so Python is the source throughout). Each condition is scored against
\emph{its own} control: renaming changes the corpus, so the conditions do not
share one. \textbf{Sample:} unlike Table~\ref{tab:crosslang}, these cells come
from the earlier uncapped run
(\texttt{results/lp4fm/summary\_renaming\_uncapped.csv}); percentages are
internally consistent but are not row-comparable with the capped table above.}
\label{tab:crosslang-rename}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
role & headroom retained & mean $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
index\_key  & 89\% & $-0.032$ \\
accumulator & 83\% & $-0.047$ \\
iterator    & \textbf{49\%} & $\mathbf{-0.195}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Index and accumulator transfer structurally: stripping every identifier in
the source costs three to five points and leaves both far above chance.
Iterator gives up roughly half its headroom---its cross-lingual signal was
substantially carried by what the variables were \emph{called}.

\paragraph{This refines, rather than contradicts, the within-language
picture.} Section~\ref{sec:index} reports index as the role that suffers most
under misleading renaming ($\Delta\mathrm{F1} = -0.272$), and
Section~\ref{sec:accum} reports accumulator \emph{improving} under its own
($+0.079$). The two manipulations are role-specific and opposite in
direction: the index condition puts accumulator-style names onto index
variables, the accumulator condition puts index-style names onto accumulator
variables. Both supply names that point the wrong way, which is what C1/C2/C4
do not do---those merely remove lexical information.

Read together, the index representation is damaged by names that actively
mislead but barely affected by names being taken away: the structural signal
alone suffices, and the lexical channel is a liability rather than a support.
A claim that index is uniformly name-dependent would be wrong; across
languages it is the most name-invariant of the three roles we test.

\paragraph{What is missing.} Two limits bound what the probe result above
can be taken to mean. Only three of XLCoST's languages share problems at rates that
permit matched transfer, so ``typologically close'' is instantiated by exactly
one pair (JavaScript/PHP) and the boundary by exactly one language (Python);
the axis is a two-point contrast, not a gradient. The overlap matrix shows
this is a property of the benchmark rather than a choice we could revisit with
more compute---the best C-family pair outside the triangle shares $175$
problems---so widening the axis requires a different parallel corpus, not a
larger run of this one. And the renaming conditions
were run on the source language only, so they say what happens when the probe
is trained on stripped names, not when it is evaluated on them.

Both trained models are $1.5$B parameters from one family. The untrained
control rules out the probe reading the input rather than the model, and the
code/non-code pair rules out code pretraining as the cause, but neither speaks
to scale: whether the gap over the untrained floor widens or narrows with model
size is untested.

We also report no interventional evidence. A probe that reads a role off the
residual stream does not establish that the model uses it, and the patching and
ablation experiments that would test this are reported separately rather than
on these cross-lingual cells.
